item.title: AI in UX: Work Is Faster, But Practitioners Have Mixed Feelings
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

We surveyed 521 UX practitioners about how they use AI at work and how it’s affecting them. The short answer: AI use is widespread and saves time, but practitioners are far from enthusiastic, and the benefits depend heavily on role, task, and workplace.

- Access was nearly universal (99%), but use of agentic AI ranged from 85% at startups to 36% at nonprofits.

- Output quality (54%) and data privacy and security (50%) were the biggest barriers to AI adoption. Only 9% reported no barriers.

- AI was used most for desk-based work, such as writing code and conducting desk research, and least for work with users.

- The average sentiment rating for feelings about AI at work was mildly positive: 3.57 out of 5. But 69% of those who chose to leave an open-ended comment expressed some negative sentiment, often about mandates and unreliable output.

- Most respondents (65%) expected their roles to remain important or grow, but researchers and designers felt significantly less job-secure than PMs.

In Their Own Words

Explore our interactive dashboard to read a curated selection of respondents’ comments on what’s frustrating about AI at work and what’s working.

AI Access Is Nearly Universal, but Agentic AI Use Is Uneven

While virtually every respondent (over 99%) had access to generative AI tools at work, most (59%) used only an approved set of tools; only 12% were free to use any tool they chose.

Agentic AI was common but not universal. When we asked which types of AI tools respondents used at work, 66% reported using at least one agentic tool: either an agentic AI product (such as Claude Cowork) or an AI coding agent/app builder (such as Cursor). Each category on its own was used by just under half of respondents (48% and 47%, respectively); roughly 30% of the participants used both categories.

Agentic-AI Adoption Differs by Organization

Agentic-AI use varied considerably by organization type. Startups and small- to mid-sized businesses used agentic AI the most (85% and 75% of the respondents working for these organizations, respectively), while nonprofits and government organizations used agentic AI the least (36% and 42%, respectively).

These findings are not surprising; government organizations tend to be especially cautious about privacy and security, which may slow their adoption of new technology. For nonprofits, cost and technical know-how may be bigger barriers. Startups, by contrast, often have few approval processes, so teams can adopt new tools quickly. Smaller headcounts provide more reason to delegate to AI, and some startups may attract people who want to work with AI. One respondent who participated in a followup interview with us told us he joined his current startup specifically because it embraced AI tools.

“I really wanted to go into a company that will be building stuff from the ground up, where AI is embedded everywhere.”

Product and Ops Professionals Reported Using Agentic AI More

Product managers and ops professionals (like DesignOps professionals) reported using agentic AI the most, while content designers and researchers used it the least.

One possible explanation is that product managers and ops roles spend much of their time orchestrating people and data across tools and systems, which is where AI agents are arguably most useful today. Researchers and content designers, on the other hand, focus on producing high-quality artifacts, such as research syntheses or UI copy, for which a general-purpose AI chatbot often suffices.

Technical comfort likely helps, too: PMs and ops professionals tend to be slightly more technical, and agentic tools still require setup and troubleshooting.

Barriers to AI Adoption

We asked respondents which factors affected their ability to adopt AI in their work (multiple answers allowed). Most respondents (80%) chose multiple factors. Only 9% of respondents reported no major barriers to adopting AI in their work.

Top Barriers to Adoption: Output Quality and Data Security

The top two reasons for not adopting AI were concerns about AI’s output quality (54% of respondents) and data security or privacy (50% of respondents). Many respondents told us in open-ended comments at the end of the survey that AI’s outputs were often not good enough or required significant time to check or correct.

“It’s been hard to incorporate AI into our workflows because we design specialty apps, and the quality of generating designs from AI is very poor / immature.”

“Using AI in my job as a UX researcher has been an experiment that’s mostly unfruitful. I tend to find [that AI] tools […] produce untrustworthy results.”

Not surprisingly, lack of executive buy-in was the factor chosen the fewest times: many respondents reported intense pressure from leadership to use the technology. As one respondent noted:

“The biggest change is the constant push from management to use it more and more. I have to actively push against them on things I know AI doesn’t do well yet.”

Many Were Concerned About the Ethical and Environmental Impact

More than a third of respondents (34%) selected ethical or sustainability concerns as a barrier to adopting AI in their work. These concerns also came up in the open-ended comments at the end of the survey, where respondents raised a range of issues: the environmental impact of data centers, AI’s effect on the job market, AI-enabled surveillance, and the use of creators’ work as training data without their consent.

For some respondents, these concerns were reason enough to avoid AI. Others described a kind of cognitive dissonance: their employers require them to use a technology they oppose on moral grounds.

“It’s a strange feeling to be forced to use something that I do not believe in.”

“I hate that I have to use something for work that I have banned my children from using. It feels complicated and gross in a way I’ve never struggled with new tech before.”…

Source: Nielsen Norman Group | Published: 2026-10-23 17:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ai-in-ux-survey-26/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=rss-syndication

item.title: Taming Typography: Building a Modern CSS Reset
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: clear, well-structured English, useful vocabulary

CSS can now make choices about type that used to sit outside a reset. text-wrap: pretty can prevent a stranded word, container query units can scale a heading to the column it occupies, and text-box can trim the half-leading built into a line box. Some of these features are experimental and browser support is uneven, so they need guardrails rather than blind inclusion.

I’ve put together tidy-typography.css, which gathers the useful parts into a default stylesheet: rendering and fallback rules, fluid sizing, vertical rhythm, wrapping, hyphenation, and OpenType detail.

Use it whole, or take the declaration that solves the particular irritation in front of you. I’ll walk you through all the details in this article and give you the full code at the end.

Rendering and fallback sanity

html {

-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;

text-rendering: optimizeLegibility;

font-synthesis: none;

-moz-text-size-adjust: none;

-webkit-text-size-adjust: none;

text-size-adjust: none;

}

body {

font-size-adjust: from-font;

}

font-synthesis: none stops a browser from inventing bold or italic when the family lacks that face. The smoothing and text-rendering declarations are rendering hints, mainly for WebKit; results still vary by platform.

text-size-adjust disables mobile font inflation that can make a deliberately sized layout jump on rotation. font-size-adjust: from-font uses font metrics to reduce the apparent size change while a fallback swaps for a webfont.

(As with other snippets in this article, this :root block is a partial excerpt the final stylesheet combines it with additional custom properties defined later on.)

Fluid typography

Viewport-based fluid type does not know how wide its element is. A heading in a narrow sidebar can therefore scale as though it fills the viewport.

.article-container {

container-type: inline-size;

}

:root {

--step-0: clamp(1rem, 0.9rem + 1cqi, 1.125rem);

--step-3: clamp(2rem, 1.6rem + 3cqi, 2.75rem);

}

container-type: inline-size makes the wrapper a container query, so its children can use cqi: a unit based on the container rather than the viewport. Replacing vw in clamp() lets the same heading scale appropriately in an article column or a 300px sidebar without component-specific media queries.

Vertical rhythm: trim the half-leading

:heading, p, blockquote, figcaption, li {

text-box-trim: trim-both;

text-box-edge: cap alphabetic;

/* shorthand: text-box: trim-both cap alphabetic; */

}

line-height includes space above the cap-height and below the baseline: half-leading. It becomes obvious when text must align tightly with another element. text-box-trim removes it, while text-box-edge measures from capital-letter caps to the alphabetic baseline. This is a metrics-aware alternative to font-specific negative-margin nudges.

@supports selector(:heading) {

:heading {

text-box: trim-both cap alphabetic;

}

}

Selectors Level 5 proposes :heading, matching h1 to h6 and [role="heading"]. It has not landed in browsers, so keep it behind an @supports selector() check.

Balanced headlines, orphan-free paragraphs

:heading, blockquote, figcaption {

text-wrap: balance;

}

p, li, dd {

text-wrap: pretty;

max-width: 65ch;

}

[contenteditable="true"] {

text-wrap: stable;

}

Default heading wrapping can leave one short final line. text-wrap: balance distributes text across its lines and works best for blocks of up to about six lines. For paragraphs, text-wrap: pretty avoids a stranded final word without balancing the whole block. Both replace JavaScript orphan fixers. Editable text needs text-wrap: stable, which prevents each new word from reshuffling the paragraph.

Hyphenation, properly tuned

<html lang="en-GB">p {

hyphens: auto;

}

hyphens: auto relies on the browser’s language dictionaries, so the document needs a correct lang attribute (for example <html lang="en-GB">). Without one the browser has no dictionary to use and won’t be able to hyphenate text. Even with the correct lang, the defaults can leave tiny word fragments or several hyphenated lines in a row.

p {

hyphens: auto;

hyphenate-limit-chars: 6 3 3; /* word length, min before break, min after break */

hyphenate-character: "‐"; /* use proper hyphen glyph instead of dash */

hyphenate-limit-lines: 2; /* no more than 2 consecutive hyphenated lines */

hyphenate-limit-zone: 8%; /* reduce overall hyphenation frequency */

hyphenate-limit-last: always; /* never hyphenate the last word of a paragraph */

/* Safari legacy equivalents */

-webkit-hyphens: auto;

-webkit-hyphenate-limit-before: 4;

-webkit-hyphenate-limit-after: 3;

-webkit-hyphenate-limit-lines: 2;

}

pre, code, var, samp, kbd, :heading {

hyphens: manual;

-webkit-hyphens: manual;

}

hyphenate-limit-chars controls the smallest breakable word and fragments; hyphenate-limit-lines prevents a ladder effect. hyphenate-limit-zone makes breaks less frequent, while hyphenate-limit-last protects the final word. Safari needs the prefixed equivalents, so declare both sets together.

Set code, variables, and headings to hyphens: manual: a broken code word can change meaning, and a hyphenated heading usually reads as an error.

Hanging punctuation and ink-aware underlines

blockquote, p {

hanging-punctuation: first allow-end last;

}

a {

text-decoration-thickness: from-font;

text-underline-offset: 0.15em;

text-decoration-skip-ink: auto;

}

Punctuation marks don’t carry the same visual weight as letters, so a quotation mark sitting at the start of a line can look slightly indented against the text below it. hanging-punctuation lets specified punctuation sit fractionally outside the text block’s edge.

The first value handles opening punctuation, and last handles closing punctuation at the end of a block, while allow-end lets punctuation hang past the right edge rather than force-wrapping. The result is a text block whose edges read as genuinely flush.…

Source: CSS-Tricks | Published: 2026-11-05 14:55 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://css-tricks.com/taming-typography-modern-css-reset/

item.title: Smashing AI Conference
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, useful vocabulary

I know there’s a lot of AI fatigue out there. I feel it, too. Most of that though is more about the noise surrounding both sides of the hype spectrum. What’s covered way less is context for where it fits best in a development workflow and what sorts of practical uses it might have to benefit — not destroy — our work.

That’s why I’m stoked to check out Smashing’s AI conference on December 1. We all know Smashing. The good folks over there check the hype luggage at the door and give these sorts of landscape-changing things careful and thoughtful consideration. All their events, not to mention their articles, are that way and always have been. The best, really.

And what makes those events the best is bringing in the best-of-the-best people to share what they’ve learned about it. In this case we’re talking about a live online event specifically about AI in design systems from some of my personal favorite people, like Brad Frost, Christine Vallaure, Vitaly Friedman, and TJ Pitre. We’re talking about people who know their craft and the experience to show (not just tell) how it translates to what we do for work, whether you’re a designer, front-ender, or even a stakeholder in the design process.

So, please join me in checking it out. Cost is €50. They’re actually giving us here at CSS-Tricks a special discount using code AITRICKSCSS when you register for the event. Even better, they gave me two free tickets I’ll give to the first two commenters on this post. Just make sure you use your real email address when signing in to comment!

Source: CSS-Tricks | Published: 2026-11-04 15:02 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Re-Implementing :nth-child() With Modern CSS
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: clear, well-structured English, useful vocabulary

The title sounds a bit strange, right? Why re-implement an existing feature, that’s completely useless! I have two reasons for that. The first reason is to be able to adjust the :nth-child() arguments on the fly.

Let’s suppose you have the following:

div:nth-child(5n + 8) {

background: red;

}

And you decide to update the 5 or the 8. The only way is to manually rewrite the selector, which isn’t ideal. We cannot have something like the below where you can change the variables as you want:

.container {

--A: 5;

--B: 8;

}

.container > div:nth-child(var(--A)*n + var(--B)) {

background: red;

}

With my implementation, you will be able to do it!

The second reason is to have fun and play with some new features. You will probably never need to rely on a dynamic :nth-child() selector, but I am sure you will learn one or two useful tricks along the way.

We will rely on the same code structure in all the examples: a container with a bunch of <div> elements inside it.

<div class="container">

<div></div>

<div></div>

<div></div>

<!-- ... -->

</div>

And the container controls the variables of :nth-child():

.container {

--A: ;

--B: ;

}

.container > div {

/* based on the values of --A and --B change the background value */

background: ??;

}

I am not saying that this structure is mandatory for the implementation. I just considered a simple one to keep things easy to follow.

:nth-child(B)

Let’s start with the simplest case, a selector that selects only one element:

div:nth-child(5) { }

I don’t think I need to explain what this selector does. The 5 is nothing but the index of the selected element. So, if B is equal to the index of the element, that element is selected.

We can translate this into the following CSS code:

.container {

--B: 5;

}

.container div {

background: if(style(sibling-index() = --B): red);

}

Is this a valid CSS code?!

Yes, it’s valid, and it works!

I am using the new if() syntax that allows me to define a condition within style(). If that condition is true, the background color is set to red. Otherwise, nothing happens.

We can also have an if/else:

.container {

--B: 5;

}

.container div {

background: if(style(sibling-index() = --B): red; else: lightblue);

}

The if() syntax is not that complex. In our case, we only have one condition, so you can see it as follows:

.container div {

background:

if(style( condition ): <color_if_condition_true>;

else: <color_if_condition_false>);

}

The tricky part is how to define the condition within style(). I wrote a small post explaining this part, so do yourself a favor and go read it before we continue: “The Hidden Trick of Style Queries and if().” It’s a quick reading with crucial details that helps you better understand how if() works. From there, you will notice that our condition can be written several ways that are all valid:

.container div {

background: if(style(sibling-index() = --B): red);

background: if(style(sibling-index() = var(--B)): red);

background: if(style(var(--B) = sibling-index()): red);

background: if(style(--B = sibling-index()): red);

}

We have our first implementation! You can easily apply it to any property as well:

.container {

--B: 5;

}

.container div {

background: if(style(sibling-index() = --B): red; else: lightblue);

color: if(style(sibling-index() = --B): white);

}

The code looks a bit redundant, which is probably one of the drawbacks of this method, but it’s still cool to implement the selector and be able to adjust the value of --B on the fly. Don’t forget that our goal is to learn new tricks, and you already have two of them in your pocket (sibling-index() and if()).

Here is an interactive demo where you can adjust the value of --B and see the changes:

:nth-child(n + B)

Let’s move to our next selector. It selects more than one element.

div:nth-child(n + 5) { }

Think for a moment about how to implement such a selector. It’s almost the same as the previous one.

You got it? I hope so!

.container {

--B: 5;

}

.container div {

background: if(style(sibling-index() >= --B): red; else: lightblue);

}

If the index of the element is greater than or equal to the value of --B, the element is selected. As simple as that!

:nth-child(-n + B)

What about this one? Easy, right? We simply use <= instead of >=!

.container {

--B: 5;

}

.container div {

background: if(style(sibling-index() <= --B): red; else: lightblue);

}

We can also easily implement a range selection, which is the combination of both selectors:

/* select any element in the range [X Y] */

div:nth-child(n + X):nth-child(-n + Y) {

background: red;

}

It translates into:

.container {

--X: ;

--Y: ;

}

.container div {

background: if(style(--X <= sibling-index() <= --Y): red);

}

The code should be self-explanatory. It’s even more intuitive than the :nth-child() notation, which requires a few minutes of deciphering if you are not used to it.

:nth-child(An)

Now let’s deal with the A argument. For example, the following selector:

div:nth-child(3n) { }

…selects the 3rd, 6th, 9th, etc. elements. Seen differently, the index of the element needs to be a multiple of 3. To do such testing, we can use the mod() function. If mod(index, 3) returns 0, it means the remainder of the division of index by 3 is equal to 0, hence, it’s a multiple of 3.

.container {

--A: 3;

}

.container div {

background: if(style(mod(sibling-index(), var(--A)) = 0): red);

}

It works! Another selector with a simple implementation.

We can identify two special cases. When --A is equal to 1, we have :nth-child(n), which selects all the elements and when it’s equal to 2, we have :nth-child(2n) which is also :nth-child(even).

While this works fine, there is a small gotcha. When A is a negative value, the selector should select nothing which is logical as all the indexes are positive, but if you try using negative values with my implementation, some elements still get selected which is wrong.…

Source: CSS-Tricks | Published: 2026-11-03 14:50 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://css-tricks.com/re-implementing-nth-child-with-modern-css/

item.title: Synthetic Users vs. Human Respondents: Same Conclusion, Less Variation
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, useful vocabulary

More teams are turning to synthetic users (AI-generated stand-ins for research participants) to run studies without recruiting real people. We’ve previously explored how synthetic users perform in interviews. This time, we wanted to test them on a more scoped task: answering a single open-ended question from a survey.

To do this, we reused a question from our earlier survey on UX terminology, in which 604 tech and design professionals told us what name they’d use for UX work. We posed the same question to 120 synthetic respondents and then compared the two datasets. Both datasets led to the same overall conclusion, but the synthetic responses varied much less than the human ones.

How the Synthetic Respondents Were Generated

We obtained the synthetic responses in February 2026 using Synthetic Users, a generative-AI-based platform that simulates research participants and their responses.

We created 120 synthetic respondents intended to represent tech and design professionals worldwide. We provided Synthetic Users with the research plan, which included the research questions, inclusion criteria, exclusion criteria, and survey questions. Synthetic Users automatically assigned each respondent a profile with characteristics such as age, location, profession, cultural background, organizational structure, and personality traits.

We requested that the synthetic respondents be asked the same open-ended question used in the original human-participant study:

Question: Which professional field or discipline do you believe best describes the following work?

An individual gathers insights about people’s needs and experiences and turns those insights into recommendations for how a product or service should be planned, built, and improved.

Please name only 1 field or discipline.

Two aspects of the platform were outside our control. First, Synthetic Users simulates interviews, so the synthetic respondents answered as if speaking to an interviewer and often gave longer answers than the humans’ survey responses. Second, the platform sometimes reworded the question — for example, asking about “people’s needs, behaviors, and experiences” rather than “people’s needs and experiences.” Such rewording is probably meant to mimic how human interviewers rephrase questions in conversation, but even small wording changes can prime respondents or shift how they interpret a question, so we cannot rule out that they influenced the synthetic responses.

These differences point to a broader limitation of synthetic-user platforms: researchers have limited control over how questions are presented and the presentation may be a confounding variable in the study.

We analyzed the synthetic and human responses the same way. Because some respondents named more than one field, we coded each response for the keywords it contained rather than forcing it into a single category.

The Synthetic and Human Data Converged on the Same Overall Result

Both datasets led to the same primary conclusion: no alternative term has displaced UX as the dominant name for this type of work.

Synthetic respondents were even more likely to use UX-related terminology than human respondents. This 14-percentage-point difference was statistically significant, but it would not change the practical conclusion of our original study: UX was clearly the dominant term in both datasets.

This difference is worth considering in context. Our human sample was recruited partly through our own channels, such as our Practitioner Panel. As we noted in the original study, the recruitment likely resulted in a sample that was especially familiar with UX terminology and that may thus overestimate how commonly the term “UX” is used among tech and design professionals.

The synthetic respondents were not recruited through these same channels and therefore did not have this particular sampling limitation. In fact, 67% of the human dataset consisted of UX professionals, compared with only 20% of the synthetic dataset. (This difference was by design: We established quotas for different professional roles when generating the synthetic sample to ensure representation across a broader range of professions. The final synthetic sample closely matched these quotas.)

In theory, the synthetic dataset offered an opportunity to represent a broader range of tech and design professionals. Yet, UX-related terminology was even more common in the synthetic data than in our already UX-familiar human sample.

We cannot determine from this comparison exactly why this happened. However, previous research on synthetic respondents has found that their answers can be more concentrated around common or expected responses, with less of the variation found among real people.

Synthetic Respondents Used a Narrower Range of Terms: Mode Collapse

The human respondents used a much wider range of terminology than the synthetic respondents. Human participants used more than 50 distinct labels, including “consumer-behavior research,” “digital-experience strategy,” “journey management,” and “human-factors engineering.” Most of these alternatives appeared only once or, at most, a few times.

Synthetic respondents, by contrast, collectively produced a much narrower set of responses. The difference was most apparent in the less-common answers: synthetic respondents produced none of the unusual or specialized terms that appeared in the human data, such as “digital management” or “business analysis.”

This pattern resembles mode collapse — a machine-learning term describing a generative model that keeps producing a narrow set of outputs instead of the full range it was trained on. (The name borrows the statistical sense of “mode”: the most common value in a dataset.)

In synthetic-users research, mode collapse refers to synthetic data that reproduces the most common data point but drops the long tail of less-common responses in the target human population.

Our synthetic respondents collapsed onto a dozen labels;…

Source: Nielsen Norman Group | Published: 2026-10-16 17:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/synthetic-users-vs-human-respondents/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=rss-syndication

item.title: UX Maps: Glossary
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful vocabulary, clear explanation

In UX, a map is a visual representation of an experience, process, or system that helps teams build a shared understanding.

UX practitioners create maps throughout a project to synthesize research, align stakeholders, uncover gaps in a service, and plan future work. Because many maps look alike, and some go by several names, it's easy to confuse them or to use the same term to mean different things.

Use this glossary as a reference to tell these maps apart and choose the one that fits your goal.

Affinity Diagram (Affinity Map)

The clustering of information, often using sticky notes, into relational groups based on similarities or themes.

- See also: landscape map

Asset Map

A high-level, chronological method of displaying and organizing all the screens and elements users encounter across channels when completing a workflow or journey, to assess its consistency.

- See also: journey map

Chronological Map

Visualization of the users’ experience over time. There are 3 types of chronological maps: experience map, service blueprint, and user-journey map.

- See also: experience map, service blueprint, journey map

Cognitive Map

A visual representation of a person’s (or a group’s) mental model for a process or concept. Cognitive mapping is free-form and can include numerous visualization methods, including bulleted lists, flowcharts, concept maps, mind maps, or affinity diagrams.

- See also: concept map, mind map, affinity diagram

Concept Map

A graph in which nodes represent concepts and labeled, directed edges illustrate relationships between them.

- See also: cognitive map, mind map

- Related article: Cognitive Maps, Mind Maps, and Concept Maps: Definitions

A visual representation of the people, organizations, products, and services that a user may interact with during a particular experience.

- See also: chronological map, process map

- Related article: Why Map in Discovery: 3 Mapping Methods

Empathy Map

It externalizes knowledge about users in order to create a shared understanding of user needs and aid in decision making.

- See also: affinity diagram

- Related article: Empathy Mapping: The First Step in Design Thinking

Experience Map

This experience does not involve a specific business or product. An experience map is used for understanding a general human behavior (as opposed to a customer-journey map, which is more specific and focused on a specific business).

- See also: journey map, service blueprint, chronological map

- Related article: UX Mapping Methods Compared: A Cheat Sheet

An expansion of the themes that a UX team owns on the product roadmap. It represents all future problems to be solved by UX (for example, related to design, research, or content) but does not include problems outside of UX (for example, in marketing, development, and support).

- See also: ux roadmap, product roadmap, specialty roadmap

- Related article: 3 Types of Roadmaps in UX and Product Design

Heatmaps are quantitative visualizations that aggregate the number and duration of eye fixations on a stimulus (UI).

- Related article: Heatmap Visualizations from Signifier Eyetracking Experiment

Interactive UX Map

A high-fidelity map that utilizes UI-design software to add interactive elements like revealing user-research data alongside specific findings or showing specific elements.

- Related article: Building Interactive UX Maps

Journey Map (User-Journey Map or Customer-Journey Map)

A visualization of the process that a person goes through to accomplish a goal.

- See also: service blueprint, experience map, chronological map, scenario map

- Related article: Journey Mapping 101

Landscape Map

- See also: affinity diagram, scenario map

- Related article: Foundational UX Workshop Activities

Mind Map

A tree that represents a central topic and its subtopics.

- Related article: Cognitive Maps, Mind Maps, and Concept Maps: Definitions

Process Map

A visual representation of a zoomed-in view on a specific user or business process, used to understand how a given process works.

- See also: user flow

- Related article: Why Map in Discovery: 3 Mapping Methods

Product Roadmap

item.title: Stop Treating CSS Container Queries Like Traditional Media Queries
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful vocabulary, clear explanation

Stop Treating CSS Container Queries Like Traditional Media Queries

To be completely honest with you, I missed the news when CSS Container Queries first shipped. And when I finally heard about it, my very first thought was, “Why exactly do I need this when media queries already exist?”

I’m not proud of that reaction, knowing what I know now, but it was comforting to know that I wasn’t alone. In fact, there are legions of us out there.

What baffles me is that container queries aren’t a new feature, as it currently sits at around 94% browser support. And yet, very few people are actually using it. According to the State of CSS survey, 86% of developers are aware of container queries, but only 41.4% actually use them. Surveys can be biased and not completely representative of our entire field, but this one is certainly the best indicator we’ve got.

Kevin Powell also talked about this at SmashingConf Amsterdam 2026: Container Queries adoption has been terrible. And that is so strange to me, knowing that the ability for components to adapt to the size of their outer container has been at the top of so many CSS wishlists over the years.

I’m not particularly interested in how many people are using container queries as much as in how they are using them. I can’t account for everyone, but from what I’ve seen — including in my own early attempts — many of us are using them wrong.

The bottom line is that incorrect use comes down to the same impression I had when learning about them: they absolutely look just like media queries at first glance. And since they look similar, it’s easy to assume they serve similar purposes and work the same way.

They don’t.

Note: I should state up front that what I’m focusing on in this article is using container size queries, i.e., a responsive design technique for responding to the size of a particular container. There are also container style queries that respond to a container’s computed styles (and are experimental at the time of this writing). You can catch up on those in Juan Diego’s piece here on Smashing Magazine where he examines their possible use cases.

Media Queries Look Outward

The viewport is a proxy. It always has been. Media queries are what gave us the illusion that screen width alone is responsible for how responsive apps adapt to their environment.

Ask yourself this: When you write @media, what are you asking the browser?

@media (min-width: 1024px) {

.card {

display: flex;

}

I, like most developers, am asking the browser: How wide is the screen right now? That’s it.

Media queries answer that beautifully, but what happens when this .card component is placed in a grid cell that’s 300px wide on a 1920px desktop screen?

The media query doesn’t care; it does its job. The viewport is still 1920px, so min-width: 1024px fires and the matched query styles are applied, even though the card only has 300px of space to work with. Eventually, everything in the card deforms, overflows, or cramps up.

“Media queries are dumb. Not dumb in terms of the concept, but dumb in that they don’t know very much. In fact, most people assume that they know more than they do.”

— Kevin Powell

It’s common to think of responsive design purely as a system for updating complete page layouts, like going from two columns on a large screen to a single column on a small screen.

Container Queries Look Inward

Container queries are smarter than that. They make responsive layouts more reliant on what’s happening inside a component rather than on the outer context that has no insight into a component’s contents. It is more like: “How much space is available for me in this specific spot, right now?”

Here is the same card code example we looked at in the last section, but with a container query:

.card-wrapper {

container-name: card;

container-type: inline-size;

}

@container card (min-width: 450px) {

.card {

display: flex;

flex-direction: row;

}

}

This changes everything. The card isn’t influenced by the viewport; its only concern is whether the .card component’s parent wrapper has at least 450px of inline (i.e., horizontal in a left-to-right writing mode) space. If that condition is true, the component goes horizontal; if not, it goes to its default block display.

“Macro” Layout Vs. “Micro” Layouts

A very interesting way to distinguish @media and @container queries is the layout type.

Media queries are for the “macro” layout; they look outward. Stuff like page structure, the header that spans the window, footers, main grid layout, system preferences (prefers-color-scheme), device capabilities (touch screens). You know, anything that is majorly true to the entire page structure.

Container queries, I’d say, are for “micro” layouts, i.e., most things that live inside the “macro” layout. We use them when any content needs to responsively fit whatever space it is allocated. Components that come to mind are things like cards, widgets, forms, navigation, and so on.

In other words, think “page layout” vs. “component layout”.

An element shouldn’t magically become “tablet-sized” just because the width exceeds an abstract width threshold like 768px. Instead, it should switch layout when it has enough space to do so, whether that happens on a mobile viewport or inside a desktop sidebar.

In case you’re still not convinced, did you know there are over 2,300 unique viewport sizes on the modern web? Do you think it is possible to account for all of them?

“

This is how it should be.

Example: Fluid Typography Inside A Component

Responsive typography is a good example of something many of us have relied on media queries for. The fact that media queries come with their own CSS units — e.g., vw, vh, and so on — that are relative to the viewport size makes media queries look really good for adjusting font size based on the user’s screen size.

.card-title {

font-size: clamp(100%, 1rem + 2vw, 24px);

}…

item.title: Building A UX ROI Case That Survives The Boardroom
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful vocabulary, clear explanation

Building A UX ROI Case That Survives The Boardroom

Storyboards don’t answer that question, and the era when a 5-minute pitch could answer it ended, unfortunately, a while ago.

These days, if you want to win budget, buy-in, and backing for UX, the design has to be provably good for the business, not only for the people using it.

And proving that takes more than taping a dollar sign to a redesign. You have to understand how your organization defines value in the first place, how it measures that value, and how a credible line gets drawn between a design initiative and an outcome leadership already cares about.

Rather than scatter tips, this article follows one worked example the whole way through. Meridian is a mid-size B2B SaaS company, and it is entirely made up — that label matters, so it gets repeated where it counts. Its onboarding redesign carries the same figures from goal-setting through cost accounting, causal testing, and the final ROI number, because a framework only becomes tangible when the numbers connect. Every step is one you can rerun inside your own organization.

Why ROI Matters More Than Ever in UX Conversations

Companies now want clarity on what every dollar buys, and “delightful user experiences” stopped clearing that bar some time ago. I still remember a former colleague celebrating a $1 million redesign he’d gotten greenlit mostly on the strength of a couple of three.js tricks. Try that pitch in front of a finance team today and see how far the particles get you.

Executives don’t hate UX, they just hate vagueness. A pitch built on “users will find it easier” loses, every time, to the department promising 12% more sales in Q3. The difference is the one between a streamlined checkout flow that reduced cart abandonment with completed purchases up 22%, and the same work rewarded with “the QA testers like it.” One of those goes on your resume. The rest of this article is about earning the first version, with Meridian’s numbers doing the work.

When Business Goals And KPIs Don’t Exist Yet

Most writing about UX ROI makes a convenient assumption: that the organization already owns clean business goals and KPIs for you to hook your work onto. Real companies are messier than that. Plenty run on ambitions like “grow faster” or “improve the customer journey” that nobody ever broke into anything measurable, and an ROI case built on that ambiguity sounds impressive right up until somebody scrutinizes it.

So the first job is often to help the organization define what success even looks like. Interview stakeholders across departments — what does product consider a good quarter, where does customer success watch users struggle, where do sales deals stall — and listen for the themes that keep resurfacing across conversations, because those recurring themes are the company’s latent business objectives. A useful forcing function is the OKR model (Objectives and Key Results), which doesn’t tolerate vagueness.

At Meridian, the stated ambition was “improve the rate of new users’ adoption of the platform,” which you can neither design toward nor measure against. Interviews turned up the real shape of the problem. Trial users needed a median of 14 days to reach first value, most churned before getting there, and onboarding questions were burying the support queue. Out of that came an OKR with actual edges: reduce median time-to-first-value from 14 days to 7 with the use of a guided setup flow, and lift trial-to-paid conversion from 8% to 9.5%.

One warning about formalizing KPIs: Impose them from inside the UX team and leadership will suspect you’ve rigged the field in your own favor, so co-create them with whoever owns the outcome — though never at the price of accepting targets that set your team up for an uncomfortable situation. Meridian’s head of product agreed that setup-completion rate was a fair proxy for onboarding usability, and customer success signed off on time-to-first-value, a number already sitting on their own dashboard.

A KPI ladder that ends at a metric somebody already watches buys you credibility before any design work starts.

Quantifying The Full Cost Of The Investment

ROI has a denominator, and the denominator is where most UX teams go wrong. You can’t calculate a return without strategic financial planning, yet cost usually gets counted as designer salaries or consulting hours and nothing else. A finance team will find the rest whether or not you counted it, so count it first.

Direct costs are the visible ones. Meridian’s redesign ran $45,000 in design and research labor plus another $8,000 in tooling and participant incentives. Licenses for Figma, UserTesting, Hotjar, analytics platforms, research incentive spend — all of it belongs in the total, and that’s before the inevitable instances of vendor lock-in every UX team eventually faces. Engineering sits in the same column, because a UX redesign doesn’t stop at the mockup. Building the guided setup took two frontend sprints plus a QA pass, $38,000 worth, and the project generated about $4,000 of coordination overhead along the way in new syncs and shared dashboards.

The line item nearly everyone misses, and the one worth stealing from this article if you steal nothing else, is stakeholder time. Workshops, design reviews, and feedback sessions all pull senior people away from their primary work. A VP of Product spending four hours a week in UX reviews is a VP not spending those hours on roadmap planning or partner negotiations. Log the attendance — who came, for how long, at what seniority — and price it at fully loaded cost, meaning salary plus benefits divided by productive hours. A quarter’s worth of workshops, reviews, and interviews at Meridian priced out at $22,000.…
